title: 7 Best Cordless Leaf Blowers in 2026: Airflow Beats Speed
h1: The 7 Best Cordless Leaf Blowers in 2026
description: The EGO LB6504 is the best cordless leaf blower for most yards at 650 CFM; the Ryobi 40V Whisper is the value pick. 7 battery blowers ranked by yard size.
dek: The EGO LB6504 is the best cordless leaf blower for most yards at 650 CFM; the Ryobi 40V Whisper is the value pick.
intro: The best cordless leaf blower for most yards is the EGO Power+ LB6504, rated at up to 650 CFM and 180 MPH on turbo, with cruise control and a 56-volt battery that runs a full line of EGO yard tools. The Ryobi 40V HP Whisper Series is the value pick and the one to choose when neighbors are close.

Battery blowers disappoint new owners for one reason more than any other: they buy on the speed number, run turbo nonstop and watch the battery die with half the lawn still covered. This guide ranks seven brushless battery blowers by yard size and battery platform, then explains CFM versus MPH, sizing, real runtime, platforms, noise and the technique that gets leaves moved on one charge.
quickAnswer: Buy the EGO LB6504 for most quarter to half acre yards, the Ryobi 40V Whisper for value and lower noise, and the Greenworks Pro 80V with two batteries for big wooded lots. Milwaukee, DeWalt and Makita owners should buy the blower that runs on batteries they already have. Small lots and patios are well served by the compact Worx LEAFJET.

sections.h: The 7 Best Cordless Leaf Blowers in 2026 at a Glance

blocks.p: Buy on airflow (CFM), not the speed number on the box. For a quarter to half acre with a few trees, the EGO LB6504 or Ryobi Whisper is the right tool. Big wooded lots should look at the Greenworks 80V with two batteries.
If you already own Milwaukee, DeWalt or Makita batteries, start with the blower that runs on them. A bare tool on packs you own is the best value in the category.

sections.h: The 7 Best Cordless Leaf Blowers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: These picks rest on manufacturer-listed airflow (CFM) and air speed (MPH), battery platform and capacity, published noise ratings where available, weight, warranty and recurring themes in owner feedback. Blowers that pair strong airflow with a platform you can grow into ranked higher. None were put through hands-on trials for this guide, and no ranking relies on measurements that were not made.

blocks.h3: Best Overall: EGO Power+ LB6504 650 CFM

blocks.p: The LB6504 is the battery blower most often recommended to people retiring a gas handheld, and the spec sheet shows why. EGO rates it at up to 650 CFM and 180 MPH on turbo, enough air to roll a mat of leaves across a lawn and clear a long driveway. A variable-speed trigger plus a cruise-control dial let you lock in a steady output for long passes without squeezing the whole time. It uses a brushless motor on EGO's 56-volt platform, so the same battery runs EGO mowers, trimmers and snow blowers. The catch is the one every high-output battery blower shares: turbo empties even a large pack quickly, so owners of bigger lots add a second battery or a backpack-style battery. With a big pack installed, it is heavier at the handle than a compact blower, though owners describe the balance as reasonable. For a typical suburban yard, it is the blower to beat.

**Pros:** Up to 650 CFM and 180 MPH rated on turbo; cruise control and variable speed; shares batteries with a full EGO yard lineup; brushless motor. **Cons:** Turbo drains large batteries fast; handle gets heavy with a big pack; kit cost climbs with battery size.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=EGO+Power%2B+LB6504+leaf+blower&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Value: Ryobi 40V HP Whisper Series 730 CFM

blocks.p: Ryobi's 40-volt HP Whisper Series blower lists airflow around 730 CFM, at the top of the handheld battery class, and it is designed to run quieter than many rivals, which matters on a street with close neighbors. A brushless motor, a variable speed dial and a turbo button cover everything from a dusty patio to a layer of wet oak leaves. Kits usually sell for less than comparable EGO and Greenworks kits, and the 40V system includes mowers, trimmers and chainsaws sold at Home Depot. The usual battery caveat applies: that much airflow uses a lot of energy, so one battery covers a mid-size yard on moderate settings rather than a full lot on turbo. It is also a large tool, and owners with smaller hands sometimes find the grip chunky. Note that Ryobi's 40V batteries do not fit its 18V ONE+ tools. For a quarter to half acre lot, it is an easy recommendation.

**Pros:** Very high listed airflow for a handheld; low-noise design; kits usually priced below rivals; broad 40V outdoor lineup. **Cons:** Bulky with a chunky grip; turbo shortens runtime sharply; 40V packs do not fit Ryobi 18V tools.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ryobi+40V+HP+Whisper+Series+730+CFM+blower&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Power: Greenworks Pro 80V 730 CFM Blower

blocks.p: Greenworks' 80-volt handheld blower sits at the top of the battery class for airflow, with Greenworks listing output around 730 CFM. That volume moves deep leaf piles across a big lawn much faster than the 18- and 20-volt blowers most people start with, and it has enough force to peel wet leaves off turf. The 80V platform covers mowers, trimmers, chainsaws, snow blowers and even riding equipment, so a property owner can standardize on one battery family. The costs are weight and battery appetite. At full output, even a high-capacity pack runs for a relatively short session, and the larger packs add noticeable heft. Buying into a new platform also costs more up front than adding a bare tool to batteries you already own. For half-acre to one-acre properties with mature trees, it is a strong way to drop gas, especially with two batteries in rotation.

**Pros:** Very high listed airflow; 80V platform covers nearly every yard tool; brushless motor; lifts wet leaves and deep piles. **Cons:** Heavy with a large battery; short runtime at full output; higher cost to enter the platform.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Greenworks+Pro+80V+730+CFM+leaf+blower&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Milwaukee Owners: Milwaukee M18 FUEL Dual Battery Blower

blocks.p: Milwaukee's M18 FUEL dual-battery blower runs on two M18 packs at once and is rated at 600 CFM and 145 MPH. If you already own a shelf of M18 batteries from drills, impact drivers and saws, it delivers near top-tier airflow without buying into a separate outdoor platform. The build reflects Milwaukee's trade focus, and the variable-speed trigger with a lock-on feature suits long passes down a driveway. Spreading two packs across the tool helps balance, though it is still heavier than a compact blower with both installed. It makes much less sense from scratch, because two high-capacity M18 batteries and a charger cost more than many complete blower kits. Its simple controls and nozzle also make it a useful shop and job-site blower for clearing sawdust off floors and decks, which adds value for tradespeople. M18 owners should look here first.

**Pros:** 600 CFM rated from two M18 packs; uses batteries many owners already have; durable trade build; lock-on for long passes. **Cons:** Expensive if you must buy batteries; heavier with two packs; needs two charged batteries to run.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Milwaukee+M18+FUEL+dual+battery+blower&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for DeWalt Owners: DeWalt 60V FLEXVOLT Handheld Blower

blocks.p: DeWalt's 60-volt FLEXVOLT handheld blower is rated at 600 CFM and 125 MPH. It runs on FLEXVOLT batteries, which also power DeWalt's 20V MAX tools at the lower voltage, so anyone with DeWalt drills and saws may already own the right pack. The variable-speed trigger and speed lock are simple to use, and the blower has the rugged, job-site feel the brand is known for. Owners commonly describe it as solid and well balanced, though the larger FLEXVOLT packs add noticeable weight at the handle. As with every high-output battery blower, runtime depends on pack size and how much time you spend at full speed, and a spare battery helps on big leaf days. FLEXVOLT packs are pricey to buy new, so the value is highest for current DeWalt owners. It handles suburban leaf cleanup, garage sweeping and job-site debris equally well.

**Pros:** 600 CFM rated airflow; FLEXVOLT packs also run 20V MAX tools; rugged build; simple variable speed and lock. **Cons:** FLEXVOLT batteries are costly to add; lower rated air speed than some rivals; heavier than compact blowers.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DeWalt+60V+FLEXVOLT+handheld+blower&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Quietest Pick: Makita XBU02 18V X2 (36V) Blower

blocks.p: Makita's XBU02 combines two 18-volt LXT batteries for 36 volts and is rated at 473 CFM and 120 MPH. Those figures are modest beside the 600-plus CFM blowers above, yet the XBU02 has stayed popular with owners who value a refined, well-balanced tool, comparatively low noise and compatibility with Makita's huge LXT lineup. It is comfortable for routine clearing of patios, walks and garages, and on small to mid-size yards it moves dry leaves capably. It is the wrong tool for a big lot buried in wet leaves, where higher airflow saves real time. Like the Milwaukee, it is a smart buy for anyone who already owns Makita batteries and a weak one for anyone who would need to buy two packs and a charger to start. If you want a quieter blower for regular tidying rather than a fall leaf battle, it fits well.

**Pros:** Refined and comfortable; comparatively quiet; runs on Makita LXT batteries; good for patios, walks and small yards. **Cons:** Lower airflow than top rivals; needs two batteries; struggles with heavy wet leaves.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Makita+XBU02+18V+X2+blower&tag=sktiger-20)

The Worx Nitro LEAFJET is a compact brushless blower that runs on two Worx 20-volt PowerShare batteries for 40 volts. Its strength is power for its size: it is shorter and lighter than a full-size handheld, which makes it pleasant on decks, patios, garages and small lawns, yet Worx lists airflow in a range that handles a typical fall leaf drop on a small lot. A turbo button adds a short burst for stubborn debris in corners. The PowerShare batteries also run a wide range of Worx yard and shop tools, so the packs rarely sit idle. It is not a big-yard blower. Runtime on turbo is short, and the smaller housing limits how much air it can move over a long session. For condos, townhouses and small suburban lots, it is the convenient blower to grab for a five-minute cleanup.

**Pros:** Compact and light; brushless with turbo boost; uses Worx PowerShare batteries; ideal for decks, patios and garages. **Cons:** Short runtime on turbo; not meant for large yards; needs two batteries.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Worx+Nitro+LEAFJET+40V+blower&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: CFM or MPH: What Makes a Battery Leaf Blower Strong?

blocks.p: Every box prints two numbers, and the bigger one is usually the less useful.
Cubic feet per minute is how much air leaves the nozzle. Volume is what moves a wide swath of leaves in each pass. A high-CFM blower clears a lawn in fewer sweeps.

Miles per hour is how fast that air travels. Speed matters for one job: getting under wet, matted leaves and debris stuck to pavement. A fast, narrow stream peels the edge up; volume then carries the pile away. A blower with huge MPH and low CFM pushes a thin stripe and wastes your time.

There is no single mandatory test that every maker uses for consumer blowers. Some list turbo figures, others sustained output. Treat ratings as broad classes, compare turbo to turbo where both are published, and use a combined force rating in newtons where a brand lists one.

People searching for the fastest or most-MPH cordless blower are usually better served by the highest CFM they can comfortably carry. That is also the answer for anyone shopping for a 600 CFM cordless leaf blower: the EGO, Ryobi, Greenworks, Milwaukee and DeWalt picks all reach that class.

blocks.h3: Trees matter as much as acreage

blocks.p: Two small ornamental trees drop a fraction of what a stand of mature oaks does. If your street disappears under leaves every November, size up a class.

Handheld battery blowers struggle on big wooded lots. That is backpack territory, either a battery backpack with a large back-mounted pack or a gas backpack. Mulching leaves into the lawn with a mower is another option on big lots, and our [best self-propelled lawn mower](/best-self-propelled-lawn-mower/) picks include strong mulchers. If you would rather pick leaves up than move them, a [leaf vacuum](/best-leaf-vacuum/) shreds them into a bag.

A high-output blower with a large pack weighs much more at the handle than a compact one, and you feel it after 30 minutes. On a small lot, a lighter blower with modest airflow is the more pleasant tool, which is why many people searching for a light or one-handed blower end up with the Worx or Makita.

sections.h: How Long Does a Cordless Leaf Blower Battery Last?

blocks.p: Blowers are the hungriest handheld yard tools, so runtime is where expectations go wrong.

Runtime claims are usually measured at the lowest speed, the setting you will use least. At full output, many high-airflow blowers run around ten to fifteen minutes on a large pack, and turbo shortens that further.

Use the lowest speed that moves what you are working on, save turbo for wet patches and stuck leaves, and use cruise control or a speed lock for steady passes. Owners of bigger lots should budget for a second battery from the start; a swap takes seconds.

Higher amp-hour packs run longer but weigh more. Some platforms sell backpack batteries or harnesses that move the weight to your shoulders. A large pack on a standard charger can take an hour or more, while rapid chargers cut that considerably.

Store packs indoors at moderate temperatures, let hot packs cool before charging, and store them partly charged over winter rather than full or empty. Do not charge a damaged or swollen pack, and let a wet one dry fully first. If you own a trimmer from our [best weed eater](/best-weed-eater/) list on the same platform, rotating packs between tools keeps them in regular use.

sections.h: Which Battery Platform Should You Buy Into?

blocks.p: A blower is often the second or third tool on a battery platform, and the platform shapes every outdoor purchase that follows.

EGO's 56-volt and Greenworks' 80-volt systems are built around outdoor equipment, including mowers, trimmers, chainsaws and snow blowers. Ryobi runs both an 18-volt ONE+ system and a separate 40-volt outdoor line.
DeWalt, Milwaukee and Makita come from the trade tool side. Their blowers make the most sense if you already own their batteries.

List the outdoor tools you expect to own in three years, such as a mower, a trimmer and a [chainsaw](/best-chainsaw/) if you have trees. Price each platform's bare tools plus two batteries against that list. The lowest total, not this week's cheapest blower kit, is usually the better deal. Avoid ending up with three chargers for three platforms.

Adapters that fit one brand's battery to another's tool can bypass battery protection electronics, void warranties and add fire risk. Stick to the maker's own batteries and chargers, and read the battery warranty, since the pack is often the most expensive part of the kit.

sections.h: Are Battery Leaf Blowers Quieter Than Gas, and When Does Gas Still Win?

blocks.p: Many battery handhelds publish ratings in the 50s to 60s dBA measured at a distance, often 50 feet, which is easier on neighbors than a gas backpack. At your ear, a high-output blower on turbo can still be loud enough to call for hearing protection over a long session. A growing number of towns restrict gas blowers or limit blower hours, and California's small off-road engine rules have phased in limits on new gas equipment sales. Check local and HOA rules before you buy.

A gas backpack still moves more air for longer than any handheld battery tool. On a two-acre wooded lot with a long gravel drive, refueling in thirty seconds beats cycling four batteries through a charger. Gas brings mixed fuel, stale-fuel carburetor problems, cold-start pulls, loud exhaust and carbon monoxide, so never run one in a closed garage.
Corded blowers are cheap, light and never run out, and some double as vacuums. The cord limits them to small properties near an outlet.
From roughly a tenth of an acre up to an acre, a good battery handheld plus a spare pack is the best fit: it starts every time, needs almost no upkeep and keeps the neighbors happy.

sections.h: How Do You Use a Leaf Blower to Clear Leaves Faster?

blocks.p: Technique saves more battery than any spec.
Check the breeze and move leaves downwind toward your collection point. Start at the house and property edges and work toward the center, then toward a single pile or tarp.

Hold the nozzle low and sweep in a steady arc as you walk. Aim at the leading edge of the pile so the leaves roll forward instead of scattering. Use a tarp to drag big piles to the curb or compost; it is faster than blowing them the whole way.
Wait for a dry afternoon if you can. If not, use high speed with a narrow nozzle aimed under the leaves, and accept that a rake or mulching mower may finish soaked mats faster.

blocks.h3: What to do with the leaves

blocks.p: Two passes of a mulching mower shred a light to moderate layer into the lawn, where it breaks down over winter. Shredded leaves make good bed mulch, and whole leaves in a wire bin become leaf mold in a year or two. Never blow leaves into the street or storm drains, which clogs drains and feeds algae downstream; many towns ban it.

Wear impact-rated safety glasses (ANSI Z87.1) and hearing protection for long sessions, and keep the nozzle pointed away from people, pets, cars and open windows. Keep the intake screen clear, check that the tube is seated firmly, and store the blower indoors.

mistakes: Air speed is the most advertised number, but airflow volume in CFM moves most leaves. A high-speed, low-volume blower makes a narrow jet that pushes a stripe of debris and wastes time on a big lawn. Compare CFM first, treat MPH as the wet-leaf number, and use combined force where a brand publishes it.

Turbo drains a battery several times faster than moderate settings, and most leaf piles move fine without it. New owners who hold turbo all session are the ones who complain about runtime. Save it for wet patches and stuck debris, and use cruise control for steady passes.
Buying a platform you will not grow into

A blower bought on sale from a brand with no mower, trimmer or chainsaw you would want leaves you with orphaned batteries. Before buying, look at the platform's outdoor lineup and choose the one that covers the tools you expect to need over the next few years.

Leaves pushed into gutters clog storm drains, cause local flooding and feed algae in streams as they rot, and many towns prohibit it. Blow leaves onto the lawn for mulching, into beds as mulch, or onto a tarp for compost or proper curbside pickup under local rules.

Blowers throw grit and small stones hard enough to injure an eye, and high-output models on turbo are loud at the operator's ear. Wear impact-rated safety glasses every time, add hearing protection for longer sessions, and keep the nozzle pointed away from people and pets.
bottomLine: For most yards, the EGO LB6504 is the cordless blower to buy, with the Ryobi 40V HP Whisper Series close behind on value and noise. Big lots with heavy tree cover should look at the Greenworks Pro 80V and plan on two batteries, and owners of Milwaukee, DeWalt or Makita packs should start with the blower that fits them. Whatever you choose, buy on CFM rather than MPH, save turbo for wet leaves, carry a spare battery in the fall, work with the wind and keep leaves out of the street.

faqs.q: What is the best cordless leaf blower?
faqs.a: The EGO Power+ LB6504 is the best cordless leaf blower for most yards. EGO rates it at up to 650 CFM and 180 MPH on turbo, it has cruise control, and its 56-volt battery runs a full line of EGO yard tools. The Ryobi 40V HP Whisper Series is the value and low-noise alternative, and the Greenworks Pro 80V suits big lots.

faqs.q: What is the best battery powered leaf blower for a big yard?
faqs.a: For a half acre to an acre with mature trees, the Greenworks Pro 80V is the strongest handheld pick, with Greenworks listing about 730 CFM. Plan on two large batteries, because full output drains even a big pack quickly. Above about an acre with heavy tree cover, a battery or gas backpack blower is usually the better tool.

faqs.q: Can a battery blower really replace a gas one?
faqs.a: For most homeowners with up to about half an acre, yes. Top handheld battery blowers list airflow comparable to many gas handhelds, start instantly and run much quieter. The limit is runtime at high output. Owners of large wooded lots may still prefer a gas or battery backpack blower, or should plan on two or three batteries.

faqs.q: How long does a cordless leaf blower battery last?
faqs.a: At full output, many high-airflow cordless blowers run around ten to fifteen minutes on a large battery, and turbo shortens that further. At the lowest setting, the same pack can last much longer. Use the lowest speed that moves your debris, save turbo for wet leaves, and keep a spare battery for big fall cleanups.

faqs.q: What CFM leaf blower do I need?
faqs.a: As a rough guide, 300 to 450 CFM suits decks, patios and small lots, 450 to 600 CFM handles most suburban yards, and 600 CFM or more is worth it for big lots and heavy leaf drops. Test methods vary between brands, so treat ratings as broad classes rather than exact rankings when you compare blowers.

faqs.q: What is the best lightweight cordless leaf blower?
faqs.a: The Worx Nitro LEAFJET is the best lightweight pick here: it is shorter and lighter than full-size handhelds and still handles a typical fall leaf drop on a small lot. The Makita XBU02 is another comfortable, well-balanced choice for Makita owners. Both suit decks, patios, garages and small yards rather than big wooded lots.

faqs.q: Are battery leaf blowers quieter than gas?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Many battery handhelds publish noise ratings in the 50s to 60s dBA measured at 50 feet, quieter than typical gas models and easier on neighbors. A high-output blower on turbo can still be loud at your ear, so hearing protection is wise for long sessions. Ryobi's Whisper Series is designed specifically for lower noise.
